query: For high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation? Specify what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, the expected observations relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation in high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings is driven by a synergistic effect between local chemical ordering within each layer and the mechanical barrier presented by the multilayer interfaces. Together, they hinder dislocation glide and delay creep by increasing the activation energy for plastic flow.
generation.material_initial_state: A multilayer high-entropy-alloy protective coating exhibiting regions of local chemical order and sharp, well-defined interlayer interfaces.
generation.intervention: Prepare and compare two sets of coatings: (1) a multilayer high-entropy-alloy coating with controlled interfaces and (2) a homogeneous single-layer coating with the same overall composition but lacking distinct interfaces.
generation.conditions: Apply accelerated creep conditions under elevated (but sub-melting) temperatures and constant mechanical loading to both coating types.
generation.structural_mediator: Interlayer boundaries in the multilayer architecture and the local chemical order (LCO) zones within individual layers.
generation.mechanism: In the multilayer coating the dislocation motion is impeded by mismatches at the interfaces and by the increased lattice friction caused by LCO. This collective mechanism forces dislocations to either pile-up or change glide path, thereby reducing the rate of time-dependent plastic deformation (creep).
generation.predicted_outcome: Under elevated temperature and constant load, the multilayer coating will show lower creep strain rates, reduced dislocation activity across interfaces, and overall improved resistance to plastic deformation in comparison to the homogeneous baseline coating.
generation.baseline: A homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy-alloy coating with an identical elemental composition but without the engineered multilayer interfaces.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be effective under temperature regimes and stress levels where dislocation-mediated plasticity predominates, and in coatings of sufficient thickness to maintain distinct multilayer interfaces.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative contributions of local chemical order versus interfacial effects in impeding dislocation motion remain uncertain without atomic-scale analysis.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of coatings – one multilayer and one homogeneous – with identical overall compositions. Subject them to extended creep testing under controlled high-temperature and constant load conditions while monitoring dislocation activity and microstructural changes in situ using high-resolution microscopy and spectroscopy.
measurements: Dislocation density and distribution near interfaces
Evolution of local chemical order via spectroscopic probes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multilayer coating does not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in creep strain rate and dislocation activity compared to the homogeneous coating under identical testing conditions, the proposed mechanism of synergistic LCO and interface blocking is falsified.

The Oxidation and Corrosion Resistance of AlCrNbSiTiN Multi-Principal Element Nitride Coatings

Abstract: Multi-principal element nitrides have great application potential in protective coatings. However, the investigation of the oxidation and corrosion resistance of multi-principal element nitride coatings is still insufficient. The synthesis and high-temperature performance of AlCrNbSiTiN multi-principal element nitride coatings fabricated through optimized arc ion plating (AIP) were explored. Leveraging the high ionization efficiency and ion kinetic energy characteristic of AIP, coatings with significantly fewer internal defects were obtained. These coatings demonstrate superior mechanical properties, including a maximum hardness of 36.5 GPa and critical crack propagation resistance (CPR) values approaching 2000 N2. Optimal coatings exhibited exceptional water vapor corrosion resistance (5.15 at% O after 200 h). The coatings prepared at −150 V had the optimal corrosion resistance, with the coating resistance and corrosion current density being 1.68 × 104 Ω·cm2 and 0.79 μA·cm−2, respectively. Creep Behavior and Its Influencing Factors in High-Entropy Superalloys: A Molecular Dynamics Simulation Study

Abstract: AbstractIn aero-engine applications, turbine blades operate under high-temperature and high-pressure thermomechanical cyclic loading conditions, which demand exceptional mechanical performance. High-entropy superalloys, characterized by a stable dual-phase γ/γ′ microstructure, have emerged as promising candidates for high-temperature structural materials due to their superior creep resistance. In this study, the creep behaviors of high-entropy superalloys are systematically investigated using molecular dynamics simulations, exploring the effects of stress, temperature, γ/γ′ lattice misfit, and γ′ volume fraction on creep deformation mechanisms. The results show that both stress and temperature significantly influence creep behavior, with temperature exerting a more dominant effect. As the applied stress increases, the dominant creep mechanism evolves from atomic diffusion to dislocation nucleation and motion, eventually leading to phase transformation. Strengthening in multi-principal element alloys with local-chemical-order roughened dislocation pathways

Abstract: High-entropy and medium-entropy alloys are presumed to have a configurational entropy as high as that of an ideally mixed solid solution (SS) of multiple elements in near-equal proportions. However, enthalpic interactions inevitably render such chemically disordered SSs rare and metastable, except at very high temperatures. Here we highlight the wide variety of local chemical ordering (LCO) that sets these concentrated SSs apart from traditional solvent-solute ones. Using atomistic simulations, we reveal that the LCO of the multi-principal-element NiCoCr SS changes with alloy processing conditions, producing a wide range of generalized planar fault energies. We show that the LCO heightens the ruggedness of the energy landscape and raises activation barriers governing dislocation activities. This influences the selection of dislocation pathways in slip, faulting, and twinning, and increases the lattice friction to dislocation motion via a nanoscale segment detrapping mechanism. Mechanically Alloyed CoCrFeNiMo0.85 High-Entropy Alloy for Corrosion Resistance Coatings

Abstract: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys could provide a solution for corrosion resistance due to their impressive properties. Solid-state processing of high purity Co, Cr, Fe, Ni and Mo metallic powders and consolidation resulted in a bulk material that was further machined into electro spark deposition electrodes. After the stainless steel substrate surface preparation, thin successive layers of the high-entropy alloy were deposited and Pull-Off testing was performed on the newly obtained coating, for a better understanding of the adhesion efficiency of this technique. Good adhesion of the coating to the substrate was proved by the test and no cracks or exfoliations were present. Corrosion resistance testing was performed in a liquid solution of 3.5 wt.% NaCl for 6 h at room temperature and the results obtained validated our hypothesis that CoCrFeNiMo0.85 high-entropy alloys could provide corrosion resistance when coating a stainless steel substrate.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, mechanical alloying, coatings, adhesion
